title: Savitr calls everyone home
hookLine: a Vedic hymn sees Savitr at evening, calling everyone home. it's why the Gayatri is kept at dawn and dusk
carry: sandhya: the gayatri at the day's two turnings
tomorrow: why is the verse called the Gayatri at all?
last: A KING WHO LEARNED TO ASK FOR LIGHT.

lines: THE POET GAVE THE HOUR A GOD.
cards: Six in the evening. A laptop lid clicks shut. Down the block, a shopkeeper rattles the shutter down.
A bus fills with people heading home, and somewhere a pot goes on the stove. Nobody announced it, but the day has turned, and everyone stops at once.
A Vedic poet watched this same hour and gave it a god, the god the Gayatri speaks to. Today: who Savitr is in the hymns.

teach.b: The Gayatri asks one thing of Savitr: may he stir our thoughts. To hear that fully, meet him in the other hymns. The Rig Veda pictures him in gold.

One hymn calls him hiranyapani, golden-handed, coming on a shining chariot and looking over the creatures of the world. He's the sun, but more than the ball of light: the power that sets things going.
A hymn in book two sees him at the other end of the day.

teach.h: AT EVENING, THE WEAVER ROLLS UP HER CLOTH.
teach.b: When Savitr comes at evening, it says, in paraphrase, the weaver rolls up the cloth she was weaving. The worker sets down a task half done. The traveler turns toward home.
The birds go back to their nests. Everything that was moving comes to rest, because Savitr has said so. So he isn't only the god of starting.
He sends the world out, and he calls it home. That's why the Gayatri isn't only a morning prayer.

teach.h: SANDHYA: PRAYER AT THE DAY'S JOININGS.
teach.b: Hindus who keep sandhya, the prayer of the joinings, say it where the day turns: at dawn, as Savitr sends everyone out, and at dusk, as he calls them back, and many at noon too.

teach.h: HE SENDS US OUT, AND CALLS US HOME.
teach.b: In plenty of homes, dusk is also when a lamp is lit. Asking this god to stir the mind isn't asking for endless motion. It's asking the one who knows when to begin and when to stop.
The weaver doesn't finish her row. She rolls up the cloth because the hour has come, and the cloth will be there tomorrow.

how: Hindus who keep sandhya recite the Gayatri at the day's turning points, dawn and dusk, so the verse to Savitr is said both as the day begins and as it closes.

games.q: what does “the gayatri in context” mean?
o: the verse heard beside its god, who stirs and stills
a verse sung only to welcome the rising sun
a hymn praising the moon at nightfall

games.q: Savitr in the hymns — tap the pairs.
p: rolls up the cloth she was weaving

s: in the Rig Veda, Savitr belongs only to sunrise
a hymn in book two sees him at evening, when work stops and everyone goes home.
hiranyapani: golden-handed, on a shining chariot.
the Gayatri is said only at sunrise
Hindus who keep sandhya say it at dawn and at dusk, the day's turnings, and many at noon too.

games.q: evening. Savitr comes. the weaver is in the middle of a row. what does the hymn say she does?
o: rolls up what she was weaving
offers the cloth to the god
games.why: she rolls up the cloth. in the hymn, Savitr's evening is the hour when everything that was moving comes to rest.

practice: For the first half of the sit, let the breath be a little fuller, as if the day were starting. Halfway through, let it go back to its own pace and picture rolling up one piece of today's work, unfinished, and setting it aside.
If you pray, keep sandhya tonight the way many Hindus do: at dusk, light a lamp if you can, and say the Gayatri or hold its meaning, may our thoughts be stirred.
If you don't pray, still mark the hour: stop, roll up the work, and let the day close.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri in context. The god it speaks to is Savitr: golden-handed, the one who sends the day out and, at evening, calls it home. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: golden-handed, a name the Rig Veda gives Savitr.

carryVoice: Your line: sandhya, the Gayatri at the day's two turnings. Savitr sends us out, and calls us home. Rest well.
